title: Indomitable Nakamura Captures 75th Bullet Brawl Title
summary:
GM Hikaru Nakamura's dynasty of dominance has been extended after he won his 75th career Bullet Brawl title on Saturday. With a score of 183, Nakamura was the convincing winner of $400 first prize.

GM Arjun Erigaisi, who was Nakamura's most dangerous challenger, finished on 168 following a streaky performance, while the Indonesian IM Yoseph Taher and GM Jeffery Xiong finished in third and fourth place, respectively.

Meanwhile, WIM Melika Mohammadi continued her own streak of dominance, winning the $100 best women's prize for the second week in a row.

The next edition of Bullet Brawl will begin on Saturday, November 28, at 12 p.m. ET / 18:00 CET / 10:30 p.m. IST.

1+0 bullet is supposed to be one of the most volatile time controls in online chess, however, Nakamura has consistently shown that he has the chops to win Bullet Brawl more often than most of the other former victors combined.

Even during natural lulls, the American kept on winning. Image: GMHikaru/Kick.

213 titled players stood in Nakamura's way on Saturday, spearheaded by Arjun, Xiong, and a slew of IM bullet specialists. After kicking off the event with a 16/18 start and winning many of his games with more than 90% accuracy, it became evident that Nakamura was in the kind of form conducive to a commanding victory.

Nakamura was particularly vicious in his first four games, winning all of them with high accuracy according to Game Review.

In one of these games, Nakamura found the most efficient conversion to complete a 40-move rout of the Armenian GM Emin Ohanyan. See if you can spot the combination that won him a rook below.

Arjun, fresh off the back of a disappointing Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 campaign, also started strongly, notching 15 wins from his first 18 games, which included a 10-game winning streak.

Arjun's 10-game streak was the best of the day.

In his first clash with Nakamura, he even managed to win after procuring an advantage with a pre-move trick in the French Defense.

Two subsequent games between the pair fell in Arjun's favor, and this was just the start of Nakamura's woes. Soon after, he went through a rough patch where he scored 0.5/4, yet, experience shone through and he managed to keep himself within striking range of the leader.

Nakamura found himself just off the pace of Arjun at the halfway mark, but you can never count out the format's GOAT. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Chess.com.

In the second half, passages of play where Nakamura scored 9.5/10 and 10/12 helped him seize the lead. Nakamura also avenged earlier losses to Arjun with two wins. The first of these, in which Nakamura employed the King's Indian Defense, featured a penetrating exchange sacrifice which exposed Arjun's king.

Volume ended up having an enormous impact on the race between the frontrunners. While Arjun and Nakamura lost and drew the same number of games, the latter won more than his rival.

Arjun fell about 10 minutes short of a huge victory. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Chess.com.

By the end of the arena, the gap had widened to 15 points, allowing Nakamura to stop queueing for new games and relish his victory. In his wake lay a highlight reel of scrambles, clippable moments moments from his Kick stream, and brilliant-laden miniatures.

title: FIDE Calls Carlsen's Forfeits 'Unacceptable,' Refers His Conduct To Ethics Commission
summary:
FIDE will refer GM Magnus Carlsen's conduct at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot to its Ethics and Disciplinary Commission (EDC), describing his forfeits as "unacceptable.” The tournament’s arbiters will also face a separate review of their handling of the incidents.

The statement, published on Saturday and signed by FIDE president Timur Turlov and its deputy president GM Viswanathan Anand, follows five forfeited games by Carlsen over the final four days in Budapest. The world number-one finished 17th after skipping Friday's fast classical game against GM Vladislav Artemiev, then winning the deciding armageddon game.

❗️FIDE Statement on the Conclusion of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026❗️ Following the conclusion of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 in Budapest, the International Chess Federation (FIDE) congratulates the medalists, GM Alireza Firouzja, GM Anish Giri, and GM Fabiano Caruana. FIDE also extends its thanks to Kjell Madland, the entire Total Chess team, and the Hungarian hosts for organizing this important pilot event ahead of the inaugural full season of the Tour in 2027. At the same time, FIDE expresses serious concern over several instances of players forfeiting scheduled games during the tournament. Some of these forfeits, including those by GM Magnus Carlsen, occurred in matches whose outcomes had already been mathematically decided. Although such actions breached the tournament regulations requiring all scheduled games to be played, they did not affect the results of the respective matches. However, GM Magnus Carlsen also forfeited three scheduled games over two days of his match against GM Vladislav Artemiev while the outcomes of the respective contests were still undecided. Such conduct undermines the principles of fair play and the fairness of the competition and is unprecedented at the highest level of professional chess. These forfeited games had a significant meaning, seriously impacting the very top of the rating standings. FIDE considers such conduct unacceptable and inconsistent with the standards of professional behavior expected of participants in official competitions. Given GM Carlsen's stature and his significant role in promoting chess, such actions are particularly concerning, as they may damage the reputation of competitions and demonstrate a lack of respect for opponents, spectators, and tournament partners. Accordingly, FIDE will refer the relevant materials to the FIDE Ethics and Disciplinary Commission (EDC) for an independent assessment of potential violations of the FIDE Ethics and Disciplinary Code. Furthermore, the officiating during the event fell short of fundamental standards, as the arbiters effectively abdicated their responsibility to uphold the FIDE Laws of Chess and tournament regulations. Accordingly, the actions of the arbiters involved will be referred to the FIDE Arbiters' Commission (ARB) and its Disciplinary Sub-Committee (DSC) for thorough examination and assessment. As the Budapest event was intended to test the competition format and regulations ahead of the 2027 season, FIDE will continue working closely with Total Chess to refine the rules governing player forfeits and their consequences in order to prevent similar incidents in the future. FIDE reaffirms its commitment to ensuring that all official competitions are conducted in accordance with the principles of fairness, sporting integrity, and respect for all participants. Timur Turlov FIDE President Viswanathan Anand FIDE Deputy President 📷 Total Chess / Michal Walusza

— International Chess Federation (@FIDE_chess) November 21, 2026

FIDE noted the difference between skipping games after a match was already decided, such as against GM Bibisara Assaubayeva, and Carlsen’s three forfeits against Artemiev: two rapid games on Thursday and the fast classical game on Friday.

"Such repeated misconduct undermines the principles of fair play and the fairness of the competition and is unprecedented at the highest level of professional chess," they noted about his forfeits against Artemiev.

Such repeated misconduct undermines the principles of fair play and the fairness of the competition and is unprecedented at the highest level of professional chess.

—FIDE statement

"FIDE considers such conduct unacceptable and inconsistent with the standards of professional behavior expected of participants in official competitions," the statement continued.

"Given GM Carlsen’s stature and his significant role in promoting chess, such actions are particularly concerning, as they may damage the reputation of competitions and demonstrate a lack of respect for opponents, spectators, and tournament partners."

FIDE also said the forfeited games had seriously affected the top of the rating standings. Unplayed games do not affect a player’s rating, meaning Carlsen’s forfeits avoided the rating risk of playing them.

Magnus Carlsen eventually won the match against Vladislav Artemiev. Photo: Total Chess.

With the case now being referred to the EDC for an independent review, Carlsen could face a disciplinary sanction, including a warning, a fine, or a suspension, if the EDC finds that he breached its code.

He has previously been sanctioned by the commission. In December 2023, the EDC fined him €10,000 for withdrawing without valid reason from the 2022 Sinquefield Cup following his loss to GM Hans Niemann. He was cleared of the three other charges in that case.

Carlsen is not the only one who could face repercussions. FIDE is also critical of the arbiters' conduct at the event, saying they had "effectively abdicated their responsibility to uphold the FIDE Laws of Chess and tournament regulations." Their actions have been referred to the FIDE Arbiters’ Commission and its Disciplinary Sub-Committee.

Carlsen also received criticism from several of his fellow grandmasters during the event. One of them was GM Fabiano Caruana, who said:

"I don't think it's good at all. I don't think it was good the first time... but this is even worse because you are leaving in the middle of the match. I think you should just forfeit the match if you don't play,” he told ChessBase India.

He later made a tennis comparison.

"To me, its like in Tennis someone decided to drop the 2nd set and come back for the 3rd set. I don't think I've seen anything like this in chess or any other sport!" - Fabiano Caruana on Magnus Carlsen not playing the Fast Classic game against Artemiev. https://t.co/JfNZQd2XFq

— ChessBase India (@ChessbaseIndia) November 21, 2026

GM Ian Nepomniachtchi went further, calling for Carlsen's removal from the event. "I think the player has to be expelled from the tournament," he said, also describing the conduct as "disrespect."

GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave described the tournament as a worthwhile experiment, but added: "I’m a bit sad that some of the players decided to make their own headlines."

Vachier-Lagrave then sharpened that criticism in a reply on X, apparently referring to Carlsen:

Correction: that a crybaby decided to make his own headlines.

— MVL (@Vachier_Lagrave) November 20, 2026

GM Levon Aronian shared a different perspective. "This event did make me melancholic and sad, but people change and sometimes not for better,” he wrote on X. "For people who are disappointed with Magnus Carlsen i want you to see his actions as a blessing for chess."

Happy to finish Total Chess Pilot. My play was not great, but it was first time we played 45+30 time control and I got to like it, even though i think 15 minutes after move 40 would greatly improve the quality of the games and still keep it exciting. Congrats to @AlirezaFirouzja and @anishgiri (especially!!) for showing amazing skills and my old buddies @FabianoCaruana and @Vachier_Lagrave for being their usual great! This event did make me melancholic and sad,but people change and sometimes not for better. For people who are disappointed with @MagnusCarlsen i want you to see his actions as a blessing for chess. New generation plays hard and shows their hunger. Look them in the eyes, they are exceptional players, intelligent and kind people. We have a world of potential and i feel that the players have the full support to make positive changes in every aspect of the game. What else do we need?

— Levon Aronian (@LevAronian) November 21, 2026

Former FIDE presidential candidate and tournament organizer Wadim Rosenstein defended Carlsen, arguing that the controversy exposed problems with the tournament’s incentives as well as questions of individual responsibility.

"I stand firmly in defence of Magnus Carlsen following the controversy at the Total Chess pilot tournament in Budapest," he wrote on X.

Rosenstein said Assaubayeva deserved an opponent and proper communication, and acknowledged the reported instruction that all scheduled games had to be played. But he questioned a system in which a player who had already secured the result could lose rating points by drawing the remaining game, while forfeiting it carried no rating cost.

"Why did the tournament regulations create a situation in which not playing was more beneficial than playing?" he asked.

I stand firmly in defence of Magnus Carlsen following the controversy at the Total Chess pilot tournament in Budapest. When senior FIDE officials, including Deputy President Anand and Advisor Sutovsky, publicly criticised Magnus for missing scheduled games, they raised legitimate questions about sporting responsibility. Anand questioned Carlsen’s decision while also acknowledging that the tournament regulations needed improvement. Sutovsky went further, publicly describing his conduct as “pathetic” and “unsportsmanlike.” Every player who sits down at the board deserves an opponent. Bibisara certainly deserved that respect, and I believe Magnus should have ensured she was informed of his decision. However, I believe we are overlooking a much bigger problem. Why did the tournament regulations create a situation in which not playing was more beneficial than playing? By the time Magnus was scheduled to face Bibisara, he had already won their match. According to the chief arbiter’s explanation, he consulted the arbiters before the game. Forfeiting the remaining game would count as a loss in the match but would not affect his classical rating. Had he played and drawn, he would still have won the match but would have lost rating points because of the rating difference. Think about that. The regulations effectively created an incentive for a player to stay away from the board rather than compete. Magnus later missed two rapid games against Vladislav and acknowledged that rating considerations influenced his decision. I am not suggesting that every decision Magnus made was correct. Nor am I ignoring the reported instruction that all scheduled games were expected to be played. But if tournament regulations create incentives that contradict the fundamental principles of sporting competition, we must examine those regulations rather than focus exclusively on criticising individual players. And this brings me to another important issue. I call upon senior FIDE officials, including Mr Anand and Mr Sutovsky, to demonstrate neutrality, professionalism and institutional responsibility. Of course, officials are entitled to personal opinions. But when someone holds a senior position in an international sports federation, their public statements carry additional weight. I find it concerning when senior officials publicly criticise athletes over controversies arising from competitions within the international chess system without placing sufficient emphasis on examining the underlying regulations. Public criticism of individual athletes should never become a substitute for institutional accountability. Their responsibility should be to identify problems, establish the facts and help improve the system. Players are expected to respect the rules. Officials mus

title: New Classic Games App In Beta, Play And Learn 10 Incredible Games!
summary:
We're excited to announce the open Beta of Classic, our new online platform featuring some of the world's most traditional and beloved games. You can now play and learn 10 games, including sudoku, mahjong, Go, solitaire, checkers, and more, all in Chess.com style.

As the app is still in Beta, you may run into bugs and rough edges while we polish things up. But getting in early also means you'll be among the first members to try this brand-new app and help shape what it becomes! Join Classic's official Discord channel to get updates, share feedback, and report any bugs you find.

Here's what you need to know about Classic:

Getting Started With Classic

Meet The 10 Games

How To Play And Learn Games

A New Challenge Every Day

Try Out Classic Now

Getting Started With Classic

Jump in on Classic's website, or grab the iOS or Android apps. Sign up for free, or log in with your Chess.com account.

Meet The 10 Games

Classic is home to 10 games. If you're a mahjong enjoyer, you can play Sichuan, Hong Kong, or American rules. If abstract strategy is your thing, you can find games like Go, shogi, xiangqi, checkers, backgammon, and word. Poker fans can also check out Gambit, our dedicated poker platform. Pick your favorite, or try something new:

Backgammon

A two-player board game played with checkers and dice. Each player has 15 checkers and must be the first to "bear off," or remove all their checkers from the board, to win.

Play

Checkers

A two-player strategy game played on an 8x8 board. Checkers move diagonally and capture by jumping over opponents. Reaching the far row crowns a checker, letting it move backward. The winner is the player who captures or blocks all enemy pieces.

Play

Go

A strategy board game where players take turns placing stones to surround territory and capture enemy stones. The player who controls more territory wins.

Play

Hearts

A four-player card game played with a standard 52-card deck. Players aim to avoid taking hearts and the queen of spades, which carry penalty points. The player with the lowest score at the end wins.

Play

Mahjong

A Chinese tile-based game. Players draw and discard tiles to build a complete hand of sets and pairs. Mahjong has different variants, and you can play Sichuan, Hong Kong, or American rules on Classic.

Play

Shogi

A chess-style game played on a 9x9 board. Players can drop captured pieces back on the board as part of their own army. The goal is to checkmate the opponent's king.

Play

Solitaire

A family of single-player card games. Players arrange cards into sequences and foundation piles, building each suit from ace to king. On Classic, you can play Klondike, FreeCell, and Spider.

Play

Sudoku

A logic-based puzzle played on a 9x9 grid divided into 3x3 boxes. Players fill in digits from one to nine so each row, column, and box contains each number exactly once.

Play

Word

A word-building game for two to four players. Players place lettered tiles on a 15x15 grid to form interlocking words. Each letter has a point value, and special squares multiply the score. The player with the highest score at the end wins.

Play

Xiangqi

A chess-style strategy game played on a 9x10 board. A river divides the board in two and affects gameplay—some pieces can't cross it, while others change behavior once they do. Checkmating the opponent's king wins the game.

Play

How To Play And Learn Games

Classic feels a lot like Chess.com. Pick a game and hit the "Play Now" button to start a match.

Face off against real players, or test your skills against bots at the difficulty you choose. Depending on the game, you can also choose settings like board size for Go, the ruleset for mahjong, the type of solitaire you want to play, and more.

If you don't know how to play a game or want to improve your skills, hit the "Learn How" button. Your virtual coach will teach you everything you need to know about any game you choose—from basic rules to advanced strategies.

Each lesson has several sections, with your coach guiding you step by step. At the end of each lesson, you'll have the chance to practice what you've learned. Just like on Chess.com, your coach will help you and can even give you hints if you're feeling stuck.

A New Challenge Every Day

If you love a good puzzle, Classic has a new one waiting for you in four games every day. Drop in daily to crack a fresh sudoku grid, clear a new mahjong puzzle, solve a new word puzzle, or beat a new solitaire deal.

Everyone gets the same puzzle each day, so you're taking on the same challenge as the whole community. Finish a word or mahjong challenge, and you can even see how you stack up against other players.

Try Out Classic Now

Whether you're a Go veteran, a sudoku mastermind, or someone who's always wanted to learn xiangqi, you now have a new place to play and meet like-minded people online. Head to Classic's website or download the iOS or Android app, log in with your Chess.com account, and start playing today!

Which Classic game is your favorite? Let us know in the comments below, and share your feedback on Discord!

title: Asian Amateur Championships 2026: Bekbol and Borisova claim blitz titles in Bangkok
summary: Kazakhstan’s Ibrahim Bekbol and Russia’s FM Ekaterina Borisova won the first titles of the Asian Amateur Chess Championships 2026 at the Bazaar Hotel in Bangkok. Hosted by the Thailand Chess Federation the competition runs from November 21 to 29. Both blitz sections were played as nine-round Swiss tournaments, with a time control of five minutes per player and a three-second increment from move one. Bekbol finished on 8/9, half a point ahead of the Philippines’ Rolly Parondo and India’s R Sham. Both scored 7½ points, with Parondo taking silver on the direct-encounter tiebreak. Blitz Open top finishers: 🥇 Ibrahim Bekbol (KAZ) – 8🥈 Rolly Parondo (PHI) – 7½🥉 R Sham (IND) – 7½ Blitz Open – complete standings Borisova dominated the women’s section winning all nine games and finished two points clear of Vietnam’s Vu Khanh Linh, who claimed silver with 7 points. Mongolia’s Dorjderem Munkh-Ayalguu earned bronze with 6½. 🥇 FM Ekaterina Borisova (RUS) – 9🥈 Vu Khanh Linh (VIE) – 7🥉 Dorjderem Munkh-Ayalguu (MGL) – 6½ Blitz Women top finishers Rapid and classical tournaments to begin shortly The rapid championships will start at 10:00 AM Bangkok time on Sunday, November 22. The nine-round standard competition will commence on Monday, November 23, with titles at stake in the U1700, U2000 and U2300 rating categories. The final standard round and closing ceremony are scheduled for Sunday, November 29. Official tournament website Regulations and playing schedule Photo albums

title: Casablanca and Oromana take early lead at Spanish Team Championship
summary:
MyInvestor Casablanca and Oromana Cen Solutions are the only teams to have won both their matches after two rounds of the Spanish Team Championship in Marbella. Casablanca lead the standings on tiebreaks following a convincing 5–1 victory over Silla Bosch Serinsys, while Oromana edged out Jaime Casas de Monzón. The eight-team competition features a strong international field, including Nihal Sarin, Parham Maghsoodloo (pictured), Nodirbek Yakubboev and Alexei Shirov. | Photo: Spanish Chess Federation

Two teams remain perfect

The 2026 Spanish Team Chess Championship (División de Honor) is taking place from 20 to 26 November at the Alanda Hotel in Marbella, Málaga. Eight clubs are competing in the country's top team competition, with seven rounds scheduled over seven consecutive days.

The championship follows a single round-robin format, with each encounter played over six boards. Teams receive 2 match points for a victory and 1 for a draw, while individual game points serve as the first tiebreak criterion. The time control is 90 minutes for 40 moves, followed by 30 additional minutes, with a 30-second increment from move one. The bottom two teams will be relegated to the First Division (Primera División).

The lineups include a number of strong international grandmasters. The highest-rated registered player is India's Nihal Sarin (2720), representing Duobeniajan Costa Cálida. He is followed by Iran's Parham Maghsoodloo (2705) and Uzbekistan's Nodirbek Yakubboev (2701), both playing for Oromana Cen Solutions.

Other notable participants include Aydin Suleymanli, Pranav Venkatesh, Pranesh M, Haik Martirosyan, Pavel Eljanov and Volodar Murzin. The Spanish contingent features Alexei Shirov, Francisco Vallejo, Jaime Santos and David Antón, while young Argentine talent Faustino Oro is part of the MyInvestor Casablanca squad.

The competition also features several prominent female players, including Nana Dzagnidze, Nino Batsiashvili, Sarasadat Khademalsharieh and Stavroula Tsolakidou. Each team's line-up must include at least one female player.

Ann Matnadze Bujiashvili is playing for FCC Medio Ambiente Benalmádena | Photo: Spanish Chess Federation

The opening round saw MyInvestor Casablanca defeat Filántropos Equigoma 4–2, with Ediz Gürel, Pranav Anand and Javier Habans scoring wins. Oromana Cen Solutions also made a winning start, edging out Duobeniaján Costa Cálida 3½–2½ thanks to victories by Yakubboev and Alan Pichot.

Casablanca and Oromana maintained their perfect records in round two. Casablanca scored a convincing 5–1 victory over Silla, with Gürel, Vallejo, Habans and Sabrina Vega all winning their games. Oromana had a tougher encounter against Jaime Casas de Monzón, securing a 3½–2½ victory thanks to wins by Maghsoodloo and Khademalsharieh.

title: Firouzja beats Giri in Armageddon to claim Total Chess Pilot title
summary:
Alireza Firouzja won the Total Chess Pilot in Budapest on Friday, defeating Anish Giri in Armageddon after the finalists had exchanged set victories. Fabiano Caruana secured third place with a straight-sets win over Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, while Hans Niemann finished fifth. Meanwhile, Magnus Carlsen forfeited a game for the fourth consecutive day before claiming seventeenth place. His decisions continued to draw criticism as the experimental tournament came to an end. | Photo: Michal Walusza / Total Chess

Caruana takes third place

Alireza Firouzja emerged as the winner of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest on Friday, defeating Anish Giri in Armageddon after the two finalists had exchanged victories in their respective sets.

Fabiano Caruana secured third place with a straight-sets victory over Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, while Hans Niemann finished fifth. The final day also brought another controversial decision by Magnus Carlsen, who forfeited a game for the fourth consecutive day before eventually securing seventeenth place.

The pilot event served as a prelude to the three-tournament Total Chess Tour scheduled for 2027, which will award two places in the 2028 Candidates Tournament. The competition introduced a format combining blitz, rapid and fast classic chess, with different scoring weights for each time control. Although the event produced plenty of closely contested matches, it also prompted questions about its format and regulations, particularly regarding the obligation to play games once a set or match had already been decided.

Chess fans of all ages following the games | Photo: Tor Nilssen

Alireza Firouzja recovered from an opening-set defeat to beat Anish Giri in the final, winning Friday's second set by a 12–8 score after having lost Thursday's opener 11–9. With the match tied at one set apiece, the title was decided in Armageddon.

The second set began with the finalists exchanging two victories each in the blitz section. Firouzja made an uncharacteristic mistake in the fourth game, leaving his bishop hanging.

The French representative recovered quickly, however, winning the first rapid encounter with the black pieces out of a King's Indian Defence. That result, worth 4 points under the tournament's scoring system, gave him a 4-point advantage.

The remaining rapid game and the fast classic encounter both ended in draws, leaving Firouzja with a 12–8 victory and forcing a sudden-death decider. Since Firouzja had collected more individual points across the two sets (21–19), he earned the right to choose his colour in Armageddon. Firouzja opted for Black, receiving 7 minutes against Giri's 10 but with draw odds. The Frenchman comfortably held the draw he needed to secure overall victory.

Speaking after the tournament, Firouzja acknowledged that the format suited his playing style, noting that it "helps me more than anyone probably". His willingness to fight through long sessions, combined with his strength at faster time controls, had served him well throughout the competition.

Anish Giri and Alireza Firouzja, the Total Chess Pilot finalists | Photo: Michal Walusza

Anish Giri interviewed by Anna Rudolf | Photo: Michal Walusza

Fabiano Caruana also completed a successful final match, defeating Maxime Vachier-Lagrave in straight sets to secure third place. After winning Thursday's opening set 11–9, the American prevailed by the narrowest of margins on Friday, scoring 10½–9½.

Caruana's second-set victory came despite a difficult start. He lost three of the four blitz games and drew the remaining encounter, giving Vachier-Lagrave a 3-point advantage heading into the rapid section.

The five-time US champion turned things around by winning the first rapid game with the white pieces, collecting four points to move ahead on the scoreboard. Draws in the remaining rapid and fast classic games were enough to secure another set victory and avoid an Armageddon decider.

Caruana's performance in Budapest also brought considerable rating gains. He earned 9.2 classical rating points and 14.0 rapid rating points over the course of the event, climbing to second place in the live classical rankings and thirteenth in rapid .

With Magnus Carlsen struggling in the fast classic format, Caruana has moved to within just 12 rating points of the Norwegian at the top of the classical rankings.

Experienced elite GMs Fabiano Caruana and Maxime Vachier-Lagrave faced off in the match for third place | Photo: Michal Walusza

Fabiano Caruana | Photo: Michal Walusza

Fifth place and beyond

The remaining placement matches produced a mixture of straight-sets victories and Armageddon deciders. Hans Niemann, who had shown consistently strong form throughout the tournament, had a less successful final day but nevertheless secured fifth place.

After winning Thursday's opening set against Jan-Krzysztof Duda, Niemann lost the second by an 11–9 score. The American then chose Black in Armageddon and held the draw he needed to finish the tournament on a positive note.

Hans Niemann | Photo: Michal Walusza

The remaining final placements were decided as follows:

Seventh place : Ian Nepomniachtchi defeated Le Quang Liem in Armageddon, winning the sudden-death encounter with the white pieces. The two-time Candidates winner had also needed a decider to reach the placement match.

Ninth place: Haik Martirosyan completed an impressive tournament by defeating Arjun Erigaisi. The Armenian was arguably the biggest overperformer in Budapest, having finished third in Group C ahead of Magnus Carlsen, among others, before beating Richard Rapport in the knockout semifinals.

Arjun Erigaisi and Haik Martirosyan | Photo: Michal Walusza

Eleventh place: Richard Rapport defeated Jorden van Foreest, winning their Armageddon encounter with the white pieces.

Thirteenth place: Wesley So got the better of his good friend Levon Aronian in Armageddon. Playing white, Aronian pushed too hard in search of a win, allowing So to secure the draw he needed with Black.

Fifteenth place: Vincent Keymer defeated Shakhriyar Mamedyarov after winning the first set and drawing the second. One of the day's lighter moments came when Mamedyarov visited the confessional booth and, instead of discussing his moves, sang Happy Birthday to his son and wished him well.

Seventeenth place: Magnus Carlsen defeated Vladislav Artemiev in Armageddon, winning with the black pieces in 55 moves. The Norwegian had won the opening set, but forfeited Friday's fast classic encounter, allowing Artemiev to level the match after a 15½–4½ second-set victory.

Nineteenth place: Andrew Hong defeated Bibisara Assaubayeva, winning both sets of their placement match.

Twenty-first place: Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu defeated Abhimanyu Mishra in two hard-fought sets, winning by scores of 15–5 and 12–8.

Twenty-third place: Nodirbek Abdusattorov finished with a straight-sets victory over Vaishali Rameshbabu.

Wesley So facing Levon Aronian | Photo: Michal Walusza

Carlsen's forfeits remain a talking point

Magnus Carlsen's decision to forfeit games continued to attract attention on the final day. After skipping fast classic encounters against Bibisara Assaubayeva on Tuesday and Wednesday, and both rapid games against Vladislav Artemiev on Thursday, the Norwegian once again declined to play Friday's final fast classic game.

This time, his decision cost him the second set against Artemiev. The Russian grandmaster had already moved ahead on the scoreboard after winning one of the rapid encounters, and Carlsen's forfeit handed him an eventual 15½–4½ victory. The result forced Armageddon, which Carlsen won with black in 55 moves.

Speaking to Norway's TV 2, Carlsen explained his frustrations with the tournament and the circumstances surrounding his participation:

What annoys me the absolute most in the chess world is that people do not believe me on what I say. I always speak exactly what I think and exactly how I intend it. [...] And it's a point in my career where I necessarily don't want to play tournaments where there's not a lot of stakes, where it's either very important or very lucrative. And here this was more stressful than fun. [...] But at the bottom of things, it was tough for me to spend two weeks here right now with wanting to be with my family. And that has become very clear, that I'd rather be home than be here. And then that has become a negative spiral for me.

The Norwegian's decisions drew further reactions from fellow participants and other prominent figures in the chess world.

Magnus Carlsen | Photo: Michal Walusza

Maxime Vachier-Lagrave, who had just completed a demanding tournament himself, expressed his disappointment:

This was very tough and I didn't have the luxury to skip games... I'm a bit sad that some of the players decided to make their own headlines.

The Frenchman subsequently issued a sharper correction on X:

Correction: that a crybaby decided to make his own headlines.

Former world champion Vishy Anand, currently serving as FIDE Deputy President, offered a more measured assessment. He acknowledged that the idea of not playing games once a match has been decided is not unusual, but drew a distinction between those situations and players choosing which games to contest while a match remains unresolved.

The concept of not playing dead rubbers does exist... It could've been explained more nicely to Bibisara for instance. But now we are in a situation where the player is deciding which games he is going to play and which he isn't - when the match has not been decided at all.

Among the possible solutions Anand mentioned were additional prize money for the final games and financial penalties for players who skip them. He stressed, however, that any decision would need to come from FIDE and Total Chess.

The organisers have indicated that they will gather feedback from players, arbiters and other parties before the full tour begins in March 2027.
